rows.en: Now we see that the first point from which the hope of the revelation of the kingdom of the Messiah went out was the time of the decline and the division of the kingdom of the house of David. But from that time no traces of it have been preserved for us in the Scriptures. Both the writers of Chronicles and the prophets from the days of Rehoboam to the days of Uzziah are silent about it. Amos was the first who speaks of it in his prophecies. Only he does not mention who the Messiah will be, nor his tribe and his stock. But he says that the fallen tabernacle of David will be raised up from the time the kingdom was divided, and they will possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations; and the captivity of Israel, which was taken captive in the wars that the kings of Judah and Israel had with their neighbours, God will bring back and plant them upon their land, and they will no more be pulled up out of their land (Amos 9:11–15). There is one ancient prophecy, perhaps more ancient than the prophecy of Amos, which, although it does not speak of the kingdom of the house of David, is the most precious, because it makes clear the final goal set for all the nations together. That prophecy is found in Isaiah and also in Micah, and it is very likely that both of them took it from an ancient prophet whose name is not stated (Rosenmüller, Hitzig). The content of this prophecy is: "And it shall come to pass in the end of days, that the mountain of the Lord's house shall be established ... and peoples shall flow unto it. And many nations shall go and say: Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and He will teach us of His ways, and we will walk in His paths; for out of Zion shall go forth the Torah ..." And after that he speaks of the perfection of justice, of judgment, of love, and of peace between man and man and between nation and nation, and of the good and the abundance of prosperity that there will be in those days (Micah 4:1–4; Isaiah 2:2–4). On the foundations of this prophecy Isaiah built his picture of the Messiah, in a sublime manner without equal. "And there shall come forth a shoot out of the stock of Jesse ... and the spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and of the fear of the Lord." He will raise up justice and faithfulness and remove wickedness and violence from the earth. He will awaken love and make peace between man and man and between nation and nation; and oppression and wickedness will no more hurt nor destroy, but the whole earth will be full of the knowledge of the Lord. "And this root of Jesse, that stands for an ensign of the peoples, unto him shall the nations seek, and his resting-place shall be glorious" (Isaiah 11:1–10). When Isaiah prophesied this prophecy, his eyes did not roam over some final time and the end of days; rather his eye and his heart were set on a man who was already among the living in his days and ready to ascend to the kingship, and this man was Hezekiah. The prophet had observed his ways and knew his talents and his spiritual and moral character, and from him he hoped for all these things: that he would restore the kingdom and its perfection as at the first, and that in his days the dispersed of Israel who had been driven away to the land of Assyria in the days of Pekah son of Remaliah would be gathered, and that he would gather the scattered of Judah, who had been scattered time after time, and especially in the days of his father Ahaz (2 Chronicles 29); and then Ephraim would not envy Judah and Judah would not vex Ephraim (Isaiah ibid. 12, 13). Therefore it is surely very likely that the prophet, when he speaks of gathering the exiles from their lands, does not lift his eyes to a distant time, with the intent of exiles in the future, but to the exiles who had already gone into exile: they are the captives of their wars with the nations and those dispersed in the lands. We see also in another prophecy how strong was the hope that Isaiah set on the reign of Hezekiah, when he says of the son who is given to us and upon whose shoulder is the government (that is, Hezekiah) that his name will be called "Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God,{v1_03_10:1} Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace; that the government may be increased, and of peace there be no end, upon the throne of David and upon his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it through justice and through righteousness" (ibid. 9:5, 6). Now in all these pictures we see that their source was the picture of the kingdom of David as it truly was and lived in their vision. The prophet Hosea too speaks of the good that is to come to the Israelite nation, and the marks of the hoped-for good are: the eternity of the nation (Hosea 2:21), its temporal happiness (ibid. 23); and then Israel will sprout and blossom as in the days of its youth and as on the day it came up out of Egypt (ibid. 17); at that time the children of Judah and Israel will be gathered together and appoint themselves one head (ibid. 2), and this head will be the king in Judah, a shoot from the roots of David (ibid. 3:5). And greater than this, we see that one prophet (the first Zechariah), of the contemporaries of Isaiah, in comparing the image of the kingdom of the Messiah to the kingdom of David, also uses, to describe the kingdom of the Messiah, expressions that are taken word for word from the expressions with which his predecessors, who lived and wrote in the days of David, described the kingdom of the house of David (Zechariah 9:10; Psalms 72:8). The prophet Zephaniah makes the chief principle of his picture the recognition of the Lord by all the peoples, that all of them call upon His name and serve Him with one consent. Only the King of Israel, the Lord, will be in their midst (Zephaniah 3:9, 15); but he does not mention a human kingdom of the house of David, just as Amos, and likewise the prophet whose words were copied into the prophecies of Isaiah and Micah, did not mention it. This spirit and this thought lie in the words of all the prophets who prophesied in the days of the kings. Seeing that all the kings who reigned in their days did not have the qualities and the virtues fit to fulfil their hope and to match the pictures that they had drawn for themselves in their vision of the happy kingdom whose coming they hoped for, they turned their faces still further to the future and prophesied the realization of this happy state in days to come. But for all of them the image and the character of the hoped-for king were one. Indeed, in all the days of these prophets, while the kingdom of Judah still stood and the strength of the nation had not yet failed to the point of ruin, this hope found the possibility of its fulfilment in the strength of the nation itself, and everything depended on their return to their moral calling, which they had on the side of religion and Torah. That is: on the side of the people's spirit, that there be a faithful will to return to the good that they had abandoned and to hold fast to it; and on the side of the king, it was required that he have spiritual talents in fitting measure and also strength of bronze to turn the steps of the people to the right way and to lead it on this way step by step to the goal of perfection. And if their calling were always before their eyes, so that the kingdom would grow strong, then their hope and the divine promise would be fulfilled of themselves, and there would be no need for wonders and signs to be done on the earth to fill the hope. Therefore we do not find that the early prophets prophesy of special wonders, of signs and portents in heaven and on earth that go out beyond the bounds of nature, that would be done at the time when the promise and the kingdom of the King Messiah, for which they hoped, would be fulfilled. It was not so in the later time. Already in the days of Jeremiah the strength of the nation was broken to destruction. They had corrupted the way of morality; faithfulness had perished and was cut off from their mouth. And there was no man who did justice, who sought kindness and righteousness. The prophets too prophesied by Baal, and the priests, those who handle the Torah, did not know the Lord. From that time all confidence was lost from the true prophets, and their eyes, which waited for the return of the good and for the renewal of an enduring kingdom in the likeness of the kingdom of the house of David, no longer roamed over the present or the near generation. Jeremiah's heart was firm and sure that the fall of the kingdom of Judah was a destruction decreed by the Lord, and that there was no more hope of upholding it; the shepherds who shepherd the people would not hold back the evil decreed against them, for they themselves were destroying the sheep of their pasture and scattering them and driving them away. Because of this evil state, and under the pressure of such deeds, the prophet despaired of all hope of the return of the kingship to the house of David in a natural way; but he hoped that in a miraculous and wondrous way the kingship would return to Zion. Not from the hand of man would salvation come to them, but only from God: He that scattered Israel will gather him and redeem him from the hand of him that is stronger than he, and will make a new covenant with them, to put His Torah in their heart (Jeremiah 31); great and hidden things He will do with them, until they are a name and a glory to all the nations of the earth (ibid. 33); and He will multiply them and make them honoured, and their children will be as of old, and their congregation will be established before Him, and He will punish their oppressors (ibid. 31);⚠1 and at that time He will cause a shoot of righteousness to grow up unto David, and Judah will be saved and Jerusalem will dwell safely, and this is the name by which she will be called: The Lord is our righteousness (ibid. 33). And Jerusalem will be called: the throne of the Lord, and all the nations will be gathered to it, to the name of the Lord, to Jerusalem (ibid. 3). Now we see that in all these acts no human hand will be in the midst, but the Lord will work great wonders to restore the kingdom of the house of David as at the first.

1.he: והרבה אותם והכבידם והיו בניו כקדם ועדתם לפניו תכון ופקד על לוחציהם (שם ל"א)
1.note: These words are Jeremiah 30:19–20, not chapter 31; reference kept as printed.

rows.en: This comes out to us even more from the words of the prophets who prophesied at the time of the exile. How they had despaired of all hope in the days of the prophet Ezekiel, and said: "Our bones are dried up, and our hope is lost" (Ezekiel 37:11). Therefore he prophesies to them that it will not be so; rather the bones will live, and He will bring them up out of their graves and bring them to their land. Already in this picture, in which the prophet likens the return of the nation to its happy state to the resurrection of the dead who have already died, a thing that cannot happen in a natural way, we see that the prophet hoped for wonders that God would do to fulfil His promise. And he speaks of the great judgments that will be done on Gog and Magog and on many peoples, with pestilence and with blood, and an overflowing rain and great hailstones, "and I will magnify Myself, and sanctify Myself, and make Myself known" among the nations (ibid. 38:18–23); and a king will arise for the house of Israel, and the kingdom will no more be divided into two kingdoms, and this king will be of the house of David, and he will be prince over them for ever (ibid. 37). In the words of one prophet whose name is not known,{v1_03_11:1} a man of this same time, the picture is drawn in miraculous images: signs and portents will be done in heaven and on earth, the sun will be turned into darkness and the moon into blood before the day of the Lord comes (Joel 3:3, 4). And how very great are the wonders that Zechariah prophesied would be done on the day when the great day comes (Zechariah 14). And in the prophecies of Malachi the coming of Elijah the prophet to announce the redemption is already spoken of.{v1_03_12:1} Such are all the pictures of the establishment of the kingdom of the Messiah among all the later prophets, and they differ from the pictures that the early prophets had; but they were one in regard to the repair of the world and the establishment of the kingdom under a righteous king from the root of David.

However, from the prophecies that were prophesied at the end of the days of the exile by a prophet whose name is not known (Isaiah 40–66), it appears that he described the matter in a manner very different from the way the prophets described it in all the days of the kings and of the Temple; indeed, his descriptions were as the time in which he prophesied asked of him. There it is not hinted, not even in one word, of the founding of a new kingdom under a ruling sceptre of the kingdom of the house of David, a shoot out of the stock of Jesse. And although he mentions the making of an everlasting covenant, "the sure mercies of David" (ibid. 56:3),⚠1 for all that we see how careful the prophet was not to speak of the establishment of the kingdom of the house of David; he makes the fulfilment of the promise depend on Cyrus king of Persia, and this king he calls a shepherd who performs the pleasure of the Lord (44:28), and likewise he calls him by the name: the Lord's anointed (45:1). And why all this? Only because those prophecies were not meant for the people of the Lord alone, but also for the Persian king, for Cyrus (see above, chapter 1), and perhaps some of them were directed to him in particular, for from him they hoped and asked that he would fulfil the word of the Lord. Not so the prophecies of Ezekiel, who also prophesied in the exile, but at a time when the wicked kingdom of Babylon still stood, and his prophecies are directed to his own people in particular. And those prophecies of that prophet whose name is not known to us, and which are ascribed to the prophet Isaiah, bore fruit in the heart of Cyrus, and he believed in them with complete faith, so much so that he said: "All the kingdoms of the earth has the Lord, the God of heaven, given me; and He has charged me to build Him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah" (Ezra 1:3).⚠2 And it is very likely that the words of Cyrus, when he says that the Lord gave him all the kingdoms and charged him to build the house, are directed to the prophecies that were appended to the book of the prophecies of Isaiah. Now after this truth and these matters, we have found one principle of faith that was founded on tradition and whose origin is from the days of the first kings. Yet the pictures of it changed from time to time according to the change of the spirit of the time, according to the ideas that ruled among the people, and also according to the demands that the time made.

1.note: The words 'the sure mercies of David' are Isaiah 55:3; the print has 56:3. Kept as printed.

2.note: The quoted words are Ezra 1:2; the print has 1:3. Kept as printed.

rows.en: From the time the kingdom was divided, "their heart was divided, and they became guilty" [Hosea 10:2]. Hardly three generations had passed since the death of David, and behold, the whole land of Judah was full of idols, and they did according to all the abominations of the nations (1 Kings 14, 15). And for many days Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without Torah [2 Chronicles 15:3], until the days of King Asa. He returned to his God and stirred up the men of Judah to seek the Lord and to do the Torah and the commandment (2 Chronicles 14:3). All that he did to restore religion he did with a whole heart, so much so that he even removed his mother from being queen-mother because she had made an abominable image for an Asherah. And with a willing soul he brought his dedicated things, of silver and of gold, and vessels, into the house of the Lord; and also the dedicated things of his father, which had formerly been brought into the temples of his idols, he dedicated to the Lord and brought them into His sanctuary (1 Kings 15). And it is not to be wondered at that he did not object to bringing into the sanctuary of the Lord vessels that had been designated for the service of other gods, and with which the priests of Baal had ministered; for we have already seen above (chapter 2), in the matter of Gideon, that in ancient times they did not consider it a sin to dedicate or to offer to the Lord a thing that had been designated for idolatry. Perhaps it was the reverse: they thought that by such an act they would make known all the more how much they despised the idols and honoured the true God. But his son Jehoshaphat did more than he to strengthen the Torah among his people. He sent teachers into all the cities of Judah to teach the people, and with them the book of the Torah of the Lord (2 Chronicles 17:9). And he set the judgment of the Torah firmly in its place: in Jerusalem he established a great court of the Levites and the priests and the heads of fathers' houses, for the judgment of the Lord and for controversies, and permanent courts in every city of the fortified cities in Judah. Over the great court in Jerusalem he set two men as heads: the one who would be the head in all matters of the Lord, and this was Amariah the priest; and the second would be the ruler of the house of Judah in all the king's matters (ibid. 19:5–11). In this appointment that Jehoshaphat made in Judah and in Jerusalem we find the first trace of an office that endured in Israel for many days, namely the office of the Pairs (Zugot), who are mentioned at a later time, who stood at the head of the great court in Jerusalem. The one was the Nasi, and he is the one whom the writer of Chronicles calls the ruler (nagid); and the second was the Av Beit Din. We will yet see in this the character of this office and the law of its heads in ancient days.{v1_03_13:1} Now at such a time, when the desire for the study of the Torah was awakened on the part of the government, this study too without doubt spread its branches and bore fruit. And now to Jehoshaphat the praise is due, that he carried the study of the Torah and of wisdom a great step forward. But the fruit of his works did not ripen, for for several generations after him the kingdom of Judah did not come to rest, at times from the pressure of enemies outside and at times from turmoil and unrest within; and also because the kings who reigned after him for more than eighty years did not truly set their hearts to strengthen the great work that Jehoshaphat had founded. Joash, who walked in the right way while guided by Jehoiada the priest, was not a man of strong moral power, and his will and also his power to act were in the hand of the priest as clay in the hand of the potter. And Amaziah his son was like him and even worse than his father. Neither of them sought the commandments of religion in truth, but only for the sight of the eyes. The service of the Lord that they upheld was only external. Their hand was with the priests, not with the prophets; therefore it came to this, until at last the king and his princes, and after them also the people of Judah, fell into the pitfalls of idolatry (2 Chronicles 24, 25). But not so was Uzziah, who reigned in place of his father Amaziah. Already at the beginning of his reign he took counsel with the prophet who had understanding in the visions of God (ibid. 23:5),⚠1 and the fruit of this act of his was seen in the land: a prophetic literature began to flourish in his time, for most of the prophets who lived in his generation and after it handled the pen of the scribe. And because he sought the Lord he prospered: he raised the horn of his rule, increased the glory of his people in temporal respects, widened the borders of his land, and built buildings like the heights. The religious, moral and intellectual state of his people also rose. And if Amos, who lived in his time, prophesied against the transgressions of Judah and against their rejecting the Torah of the Lord (Amos 2:4), this is not to be wondered at in our eyes, for so it was at the beginning of his reign, for the moral state of a people is not overturned in one day. And although the king's efforts to turn many away from iniquity were great, not all of them returned. The high and the princes did not know how to do good (Hosea 5:10). But if on the one side the prophets of that time had a controversy with Judah too (ibid. 12:3), on the other side they set their hope in Judah, that the saviour of Israel would go out from its midst, that under his sceptre the fallen tabernacle of David would be raised up, to wall up the breaches and to raise up the ruins (Amos 9:11); and there is no doubt⚠2 that the prophet supported this hope of his on the reign of King Uzziah. But this hope was not fulfilled. The relief that Israel had under his rule became, at the end of his days, the ruin of morality in the people. For the increase of wealth and of good among the people worked for evil with the masses, who stood on a low level of enlightenment, and they bred pride of heart, love of pleasures, and also iniquity and violence. The prophecy that Isaiah prophesied in the year that Uzziah died is full of these traces, when the prophet tells them that all hope of improving them is lost, until they perish and nothing remains of them but a small remnant (Isaiah 6). The success that Uzziah had during the days of his long reign came to him because his hand was always with the prophets. But to the priests he showed no favour, and they too were not his friends. Once he came into the temple of the Lord and burned incense on the altar of incense, and behold, Azariah the priest, and with him eighty priests, valiant men, were angry with him and said to him: "It pertains not unto you, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the Lord ... go out of the sanctuary, for you have trespassed" (2 Chronicles 26:16–18). Perhaps the priests saw a trespass in this deed because they thought that Uzziah wished to use the crown of priesthood, as was done among the Assyrians and the other kings of the East, where the king is the chief priest. But if we consider the ways of Uzziah, it was not so.{v1_03_14:1} Rather, what he did he did only in his simplicity, his righteousness and the uprightness of his heart. He saw, and also knew, that the first righteous kings had also done so and burned incense on the altar of the Lord, not to commit a trespass against the Lord but to give honour to the name of the Lord; and how was he lower than they, that he should not do so? And for the aim of our inquiry we see in this a new proof that the ancients did not object to departing from the form of the law, if its intent and its spirit were not corrupted by their deeds. Through the quarrel of the priests with the king a great evil came about. His son Jotham kept away from coming into the house of the Lord, and the end of this was that "the people did yet corruptly" (2 Chronicles 27:2). But this separation became in the course of the days a curse to the whole people of Judah. Death hurried Jotham away in the middle of the course of his life, and he was no more. And quickly all the good things of religion, of morality and of his people were lost, and they were as though they had not been. His son Ahaz came to the kingship after him, and he corrupted his way more than all who had been before him; and with the moral corruption the temporal good also vanished from the land. Already at the end of the days of Jotham the king of Aram and the king of Israel conspired against him (2 Kings 15:37), and in the days of Ahaz the conspiracy grew strong, and they came into the land of Judah and laid it waste, except Jerusalem, which they could not overcome (ibid. 16:5). The inner moral and religious state the prophet Isaiah describes in a very terrible manner (Isaiah 1). But there is one thing among his rebukes that throws light on the character of their way in keeping religion. For although they went astray from the way of understanding, to go astray after other gods, and moreover broke loose in their morals and their corruption was in them, for all that they did not abolish the service of the sacrifices; and while they abandoned faithfulness, justice and righteousness, they did not cease from doing statutory acts, without paying heed to the purpose these were designed to attain, nor to the spirit and the morality in them. And against these contradictions Isaiah rebuked them, saying that this is not the Torah of our God. For God does not desire the multitude of their sacrifices, and does not ask that they come to appear before Him; rather their meal-offering and their incense are an abomination to Him; also the new moon and the sabbath, the calling of assemblies, His soul hates [Isaiah 1:11–14]. And why all this? Because He cannot endure iniquity along with the solemn assembly.{v1_03_14:2} And what is it that the Lord requires of them? Purity of heart, and the seeking of justice, judgment and uprightness. If we turn our gaze to the land of the kingdom of Israel, we meet this same sight too. In all the history of that kingdom, from the day it was founded until it perished from the earth, we see that they transgressed the teachings; there was no faithfulness and no morality among them, but they did abominable deeds, adding sin to sin; and for all that they held on to the customs of their fathers and lived by the external acts of the Torah, and especially by the service of the sacrifices. For otherwise, how could the prophet Hosea have rebuked the priests, saying: "They feed on the sin of My people, and set their heart on their iniquity" (Hosea 4:8)? In this is described the perverseness of thought in which they were ensnared through the guilt of the priests, who wished out of love of gain that the people should sin, so that they would bring their sin-offerings and the priests would eat them. And he complains against the people, who think that by their sacrifices they will attain God's favour, and who go with their flocks and with their herds to seek the Lord (ibid. 5:6). And two and three times this prophet rebukes them about the doing of external acts without any heed to the inner intent. And like him the prophet Amos too, who prophesied one generation before Hosea in the land of Israel, complains against the men of his generation about this perverseness. And how fine is his mockery of those who keep the sabbath and the new moon while their eyes are not on justice and faithfulness, who say: "When will the sabbath and the new moon be gone, that we may do our work," "that we may sell grain, and set forth corn." And why do they ask this? So that after the new moon and the sabbath they can "make the ephah small," "falsify the balances of deceit," and "buy the poor for silver" (Amos 5:5, 6).⚠3 Now we have seen that this moral sickness was common to the two kingdoms together; and therefore it is no longer to be wondered at that under the reign of Ahaz, who served other gods and did according to all the abominations of the nations, and like king like people, they abandoned the qualities of the Israelite religion and "strike hands with the children of strangers" (Isaiah 3),⚠4 and that for all that they were strict about the external acts, and especially about the practice of the sacrifices (2 Kings 16:11–15).

1.note: Uzziah's counsel with the prophet is 2 Chronicles 26:5; the print reads כ"ג (23:5). Kept as printed.

2.note: Word printed לפון, not a usual expression; read as 'there is no doubt' (perhaps for לפקפק or ספק).

3.note: The quoted verses are Amos 8:5–6; the print has 5:5, 6. Kept as printed.

4.note: The phrase 'strike hands with the children of strangers' is Isaiah 2:6, not chapter 3. Kept as printed.

footnotes.en: All the commentators agree that this prophecy is directed to Hezekiah, and it seems that the epithet "Mighty God" (El gibbor) is nothing but a rendering of the name "Hezekiah" in other words.

If we consider the last two sections of the book of Joel, we find that they have no proper connection at all with the preceding ones. For the preceding ones speak of the evil that came upon the land from the locust and the palmerworm, which made everything a desolation, and the prophet calls to repentance and promises that when they return the Lord will have pity on His people, and they will know through this that the Lord is God. But the last ones do not speak of this event at all; they are only prophecies about future time. And the prophet speaks of the return of the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, and of their scattering among the nations and the division of the land, which already existed in fact. He speaks also of their precious things that were brought into the temples (Ezra 1:7), and he speaks of those sold to the sons of the Greeks. And all these are matters that were certainly and clearly not prophesied before the destruction of the Temple. See further on this in *Moreh Nevukhei ha-Zeman*, gate 11.

Indeed it seems that the ending of the book of Malachi is not part of the book; rather the last verses, "Remember the Torah of Moses My servant ... Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet" [Malachi 3:22–23], are the conclusion of the collection of the Torah and the Prophets. And the epithet "Elijah the prophet" does not refer to the ancient Elijah; rather it calls the prophet in general by the name Elijah, just as Ezekiel (37:24) called the king who will arise by the name "My servant David." And it is likely that this conclusion is from a time when they complained most about the cessation of prophecy. See in Psalms chapter 74, the whole of which psalm shows that it was composed in the time of the Hasmoneans, and there it complains of this: "We see not our signs; there is no more any prophet; neither is there among us any that knows how long" [Psalms 74:9]. And in several places in the book of the Hasmoneans the expression is found, "until a prophet arises in Israel," or "until a true prophet arises in Israel." And according to this we may suppose that this conclusion was made at that time, that is, at the time when Judah Maccabee, after he had prevailed, gathered the holy writings that had been scattered in the days of the war and the persecution, as is explained in the Second Book of the Hasmoneans; then they made this conclusion to seal his collection.

My brother-in-law,⚠1 the Rabbi R. Ḥayyim Oppenheim, drew my attention to this inquiry, and he treated it at length in a special article that he wrote about the Pairs (Zugot), their character and their history.

1.note: First letter unclear in the print (ג or נ); read גיסי, 'my brother-in-law'.
